tcpCongestion.title: TCP Flow & Congestion Control (cwnd & Sliding Window)
tcpCongestion.subtitle: Visualize Congestion Window (cwnd) dynamics: Slow Start exponential growth, Congestion Avoidance AIMD, and Fast Recovery packet loss collapse.
tcpCongestion.mentalModel: TCP constantly probes network capacity by doubling cwnd during Slow Start, increasing by +1 MSS per RTT during Congestion Avoidance, and halving/collapsing cwnd on packet loss.

failureModes: Bufferbloat: Excessively large router queue buffers delay packet loss signals, causing RTT to swell to multi-second delays while TCP cwnd remains artificially high.
Global Synchronization: In networks with tail-drop queues, multiple TCP flows drop packets simultaneously, causing all connections to collapse cwnd to 1 MSS at the exact same moment.
tradeOffs: TCP Reno vs CUBIC vs BBR: Reno/CUBIC use loss-based congestion detection (collapsing cwnd on packet loss). Google's BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and RTT) uses delay-based pacing, maximizing throughput without filling router buffers.
theoryData.productionScenario: A cross-region microservice communication pipeline experienced throughput degradation over 100ms RTT links. Tuning Linux TCP socket buffers (`sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_rmem='4096 87380 16777216'`) allowed the sliding receiver window (rwnd) to scale to 16MB, utilizing full 10Gbps link capacity.

interviewQA.q: What is the difference between TCP Flow Control and TCP Congestion Control?
interviewQA.a: Flow Control prevents the sender from overwhelming the RECEIVER's buffer (regulated by `rwnd` advertised in TCP headers). Congestion Control prevents senders from overwhelming the NETWORK (regulated by `cwnd` estimated via packet loss/delay).

quizData.question: In TCP Slow Start, if cwnd = 1 MSS initially, how many MSS packets are sent in the 4th Round Trip Time (RTT)?
quizData.answer: In Slow Start, cwnd doubles every RTT (1 -> 2 -> 4 -> 8). In the 4th RTT, cwnd = 8 MSS packets.

consistentHashing.title: Consistent Hashing & Ring Rebalancing
consistentHashing.subtitle: Visualize 360-degree hash ring distribution, node placement, virtual nodes, and minimal key re-mapping during server node additions or crashes.
consistentHashing.mentalModel: Consistent hashing maps both server nodes and keys onto a circular hash ring — when a server is added or fails, only 1/N of keys are remapped instead of all keys.

failureModes: Hotspotting / Non-Uniform Key Distribution: Without Virtual Nodes, servers receive uneven key loads on the ring, overloading individual cache nodes.
Cascading Cache Failures: When one cache node dies, its entire key workload dumps onto its immediate clockwise neighbor, causing it to crash as well.
tradeOffs: Naive Modulo Hashing `hash(key) % N` vs Consistent Hashing: Modulo hashing remaps ~100% of keys whenever N changes (catastrophic for distributed caches like Redis/Memcached). Consistent hashing remaps only $K/N$ keys.
theoryData.productionScenario: A distributed caching cluster with 20 nodes experienced database outages whenever a node was added. Switching from modulo hashing to Consistent Hashing with 150 Virtual Nodes per physical server reduced key cache invalidations from 95% to 4.8%.

interviewQA.q: Why are Virtual Nodes necessary in Consistent Hashing?
interviewQA.a: Virtual Nodes map each physical server to multiple positions (e.g. 100-200 points) across the hash ring. This ensures balanced key distribution and spreads a failed node's workload evenly across ALL remaining physical servers rather than overloading just one neighbor.

quizData.question: If a Consistent Hash ring has 10 physical servers and 1 server fails, what percentage of keys must be remapped?
quizData.answer: Only approximately 1/10 (10%) of the keys (the ones that belonged to the failed server) need to be remapped to remaining servers.
